Additionally, they submit that the RPD decision cannot stand in light of new evidence that they have disclosed on appeal to the RAD.

[7] Subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA)3 states that an appellant may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of their claim or that was not reasonably available, or that they could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented at the time of the rejection. It is for the appellant to provide full and detailed submissions in their memorandum about how any proposed new evidence meets the requirements of subsection 110(4) of the IRPA and how that evidence relates to them.

[8] If the new evidence meets the requirements in subsection 110(4) of the IRPA, then the RAD must also apply the adapted Raza factors endorsed in Singh. In Singh, the Federal Court of Appeal held that the RAD should assess the admissibility of the new evidence for its credibility, relevance, and newness.4
The new evidence is rejected

[9] The Appellant submits one item5 of new evidence:
* Letter from the Appellant's sister, dated XXXX XXXX, 2023.6

[10] The Appellant has also provided an affidavit to support the new evidence. Although I consider this affidavit to be submissions and not new evidence, I have taken it into consideration in assessing the admissibility of his sister's letter.

[11] I find that the letter from the Appellant's sister does not meet the requirements of subsection 110(4) of the IRPA.

[12] Although the letter is dated after the RPD decision, it concerns a pattern of events that occurred before the RPD hearing and decision. The author of the letter states that she received three calls from the CJNG on XXXX XXXX, 2022 (XXXX XXXX XXXX before the RPD hearing), XXXX XXXX, 2022 (XXXX months before the RPD hearing), and XXXX XXXX, 2023 (XXXX days after the RPD decision). She writes that the purpose of these calls was to threaten the PA for not paying the ransom and violating the interests of the group. The letter also states that she added these facts to the police investigation file and gives reasons why she was unable to provide supporting proof of this.

[13] The Appellants submit that this evidence was not reasonably available, or that they could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented it at the time of the rejection, because they only learned about these events and the identity of the APH when the PA's sister told them after the RPD decision, when the PA communicated to her that their claim had been rejected. The Appellant's sister writes in her letter that she did not tell her brother about these calls "so as not to worry him since he had many problems due to everything that had happened to him, his stress, anxiety and vitiligo problems..."7

[14] Respectfully, I find that this explanation is not credible. The PA testified that he is in regular contact with his family in Mexico. He communicates with them by phone every two weeks.8 His family consists of his parents, two sisters, and one brother.9 He last spoke with them a few days before the RPD hearing.10 The PA's sister who wrote the letter was initially contacted by the APH in early 2021 who demanded a ransom for the Appellants' release. She is therefore knowledgeable of the Appellants' targeting by the APH and has been since before they made their claim for refugee protection in Canada. On a balance of probabilities, I find that the PA's sister and family members were aware of the Appellants' decision to seek refuge in Canada in XXXX 2021, and supported it.

[15] Under the circumstances, I find that it is not credible that the PA's sister would not have informed the Appellants or their mutual family members about the multiple calls that she received from the APH until after she learned about their rejection by the RPD. If what she alleges in her letter is true, she would have informed them immediately, or as soon as possible. The PA's sister clearly supports a positive outcome for their claim, as evidenced by her letter and other efforts on their behalf to obtain documentation for their claim. The calls were death threats directed against the PA. There is no evidence that the PA's sister had received any other communication from the APH after XXXX 2021 despite not paying the ransom. The PA's sister learned through these calls that the APH were the CJNG, widely known to be one of Mexico's most violent and powerful cartels, whereas previously the identity of the APH was unknown. She was so concerned about these calls that she moved and changed her number after the second call in XXXX 2022. Therefore, these calls represented an alarming escalation in the potential risk to the Appellants and the PA's family, months before the RPD hearing. Despite this, and despite the PA having roughly a dozen phone conversations with his family members in Mexico after the CJNG allegedly first contacted his sister in XXXX 2022, the Appellants are asking the RAD to accept that the PA did not learn about these calls or the identity of the APH until after their rejection by the RPD. Respectfully, this is implausible.

[18] Furthermore, I find that this evidence is not sufficiently credible or trustworthy to be admissible. The jurisprudence supports that suspicious and fortuitous timing with respect to new evidence may, in limited circumstances, support a finding that it is not credible or trustworthy.13 I find that it is an extraordinary coincidence that the Appellants learned the identity of the APH and that the APH had suddenly escalated their apparent efforts to find them, just after their rejection by the RPD. This new evidence is extraordinarily fortuitous in that it directly responds to two of the main adverse findings by the RPD, that the Appellants did not know the identity of the criminal organization that targeted them, and that there was no evidence that the APH approached their family members to find them. If the new evidence is to be believed, the APH began persistently targeting the Appellants' family members more than a year after the Appellants' last interaction with them, and finally revealed themselves to be part of one of Mexico's most notorious cartels roughly two years after they began targeting the PA for extortion. Also, they located the PA's sister a few days after the RPD decision, even though she had moved and changed her number. These are sudden and unexplained developments that are so coincidental for the Appellants' claim that they must be treated with suspicion. This is in addition to the concerns I have identified above concerning the Appellants' explanation for not providing the evidence at the time of the RPD decision, which raise doubts about whether the events in question occurred. Overall, I find that the PA's letter is not sufficiently credible or trustworthy to be admitted.

[19] I accept that the letter is a sworn statement, however for the reasons provided herein, I find that there are good reasons to doubt the truthfulness of its contents.

[20] Therefore, I find that this evidence does not meet the requirements of s. 110(4) of the IRPA and I do not admit it.

[23] My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision after conducting an independent assessment.15

[24] The determinative issue in this claim is an IFA in Mérida, Yucatán.

[26] They submit that as they were self-represented at the time, and the Immigration and Refugee Board should have provided a "screening form" to the Appellants before the RPD hearing which identified the relevant issues.

Evidence in the National Document Package corroborates that feminicide, the intentional killing of women because they are women, is a serious and persistent human rights problem affecting every state in Mexico,35 and that there is frequently impunity for perpetrators.36

REASONS FOR DECISION
OVERVIEW
[1] I dismiss the appeal of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (Principal Appellant) and XXXX XXXX XXXX (Associate Appellant), citizens of Mexico.
[2] The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) was correct in finding that the Appellants are neither Convention1 refugees nor persons in need of protection.

[3] The following is a brief (and non-exhaustive) summary of the Appellants' allegations in their Basis of Claim (BOC) forms and narrative:
* The Appellants fear a criminal gang/organization ("agents of persecution or harm" or "APH") in the state of Morelos, Mexico.
* The Principal Appellant (PA) was the victim of attempted extortion by the APH in XXXX 2020, when he was living in Jiutepec, Morelos, working in the family XXXX XXXX business.
* He moved to XXXX, Morelos, in XXXX 2022.
* On XXXX XXXX, 2022, the Appellants were kidnapped, abused, and threatened by the APH. The kidnappers demanded a XXXX XXXX XXXX pesos ransom from the PA's sister, however the Appellants managed to escape two days after their abduction.
* They filed a case with the local police, and the PA closed his family XXXX XXXX business.
* The Appellants left Mexico on XXXX XXXX, 2022, and claimed refugee protection in Canada upon arrival.
* On Appeal to the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD), the Appellants submit that new evidence has come to light that the agents of persecution or harm belong to the Cártel de Jalisco Nueva Generación (CJNG).

[4] The determinative issue for the RPD was an Internal Flight Alternative (IFA) in Mérida, in the state of Yucatán. Applying the two-pronged test for an IFA established by the Federal Court of Appeal in Rasaratnam,2 the RPD concluded that the Appellants failed to establish that the criminal gang/organization who targeted them in Morelos possessed the motivation to pursue them to the IFA and that they did not demonstrate that the IFA would be objectively unreasonable in all the circumstances.

[5] The Appellants, who were unrepresented before the RPD, argue that the RPD violated procedural fairness or natural justice by failing to provide them with notice that it was considering Mérida as a possible IFA. They also argue that the RPD made fatal errors in its assessment under both prongs of the IFA test with regards to the evidence that was before it, including the objective documentary evidence. Additionally, they submit that the RPD decision cannot stand in light of new evidence that they have disclosed on appeal to the RAD.

[6] I find that there was no violation of procedural fairness or natural justice, and that the RPD was correct to determine that the Appellants have a viable IFA in Mérida, Yucatán. The RPD decision is correct.
NEW EVIDENCE

[7] Subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA)3 states that an appellant may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of their claim or that was not reasonably available, or that they could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented at the time of the rejection. It is for the appellant to provide full and detailed submissions in their memorandum about how any proposed new evidence meets the requirements of subsection 110(4) of the IRPA and how that evidence relates to them.

[8] If the new evidence meets the requirements in subsection 110(4) of the IRPA, then the RAD must also apply the adapted Raza factors endorsed in Singh. In Singh, the Federal Court of Appeal held that the RAD should assess the admissibility of the new evidence for its credibility, relevance, and newness.4
The new evidence is rejected

[9] The Appellant submits one item5 of new evidence:
* Letter from the Appellant's sister, dated XXXX XXXX, 2023.6

[10] The Appellant has also provided an affidavit to support the new evidence. Although I consider this affidavit to be submissions and not new evidence, I have taken it into consideration in assessing the admissibility of his sister's letter.
[11] I find that the letter from the Appellant's sister does not meet the requirements of subsection 110(4) of the IRPA.

[12] Although the letter is dated after the RPD decision, it concerns a pattern of events that occurred before the RPD hearing and decision. The author of the letter states that she received three calls from the CJNG on XXXX XXXX, 2022 (XXXX XXXX XXXX before the RPD hearing), XXXX XXXX, 2022 (XXXX months before the RPD hearing), and XXXX XXXX, 2023 (XXXX days after the RPD decision). She writes that the purpose of these calls was to threaten the PA for not paying the ransom and violating the interests of the group. The letter also states that she added these facts to the police investigation file and gives reasons why she was unable to provide supporting proof of this.

[13] The Appellants submit that this evidence was not reasonably available, or that they could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented it at the time of the rejection, because they only learned about these events and the identity of the APH when the PA's sister told them after the RPD decision, when the PA communicated to her that their claim had been rejected. The Appellant's sister writes in her letter that she did not tell her brother about these calls "so as not to worry him since he had many problems due to everything that had happened to him, his stress, anxiety and vitiligo problems..."7

[14] Respectfully, I find that this explanation is not credible. The PA testified that he is in regular contact with his family in Mexico. He communicates with them by phone every two weeks.8 His family consists of his parents, two sisters, and one brother.9 He last spoke with them a few days before the RPD hearing.10 The PA's sister who wrote the letter was initially contacted by the APH in early 2021 who demanded a ransom for the Appellants' release. She is therefore knowledgeable of the Appellants' targeting by the APH and has been since before they made their claim for refugee protection in Canada. On a balance of probabilities, I find that the PA's sister and family members were aware of the Appellants' decision to seek refuge in Canada in XXXX 2021, and supported it.

[15] Under the circumstances, I find that it is not credible that the PA's sister would not have informed the Appellants or their mutual family members about the multiple calls that she received from the APH until after she learned about their rejection by the RPD. If what she alleges in her letter is true, she would have informed them immediately, or as soon as possible. The PA's sister clearly supports a positive outcome for their claim, as evidenced by her letter and other efforts on their behalf to obtain documentation for their claim. The calls were death threats directed against the PA. There is no evidence that the PA's sister had received any other communication from the APH after XXXX 2021 despite not paying the ransom. The PA's sister learned through these calls that the APH were the CJNG, widely known to be one of Mexico's most violent and powerful cartels, whereas previously the identity of the APH was unknown. She was so concerned about these calls that she moved and changed her number after the second call in XXXX 2022. Therefore, these calls represented an alarming escalation in the potential risk to the Appellants and the PA's family, months before the RPD hearing. Despite this, and despite the PA having roughly a dozen phone conversations with his family members in Mexico after the CJNG allegedly first contacted his sister in XXXX 2022, the Appellants are asking the RAD to accept that the PA did not learn about these calls or the identity of the APH until after their rejection by the RPD. Respectfully, this is implausible.

[16] Plausibility findings should only be made in the "clearest of cases" and with caution, given concerns about subjectivity and cultural context. The RPD and RAD may draw conclusions on credibility based on implausibility, rationality, and common sense.11 While the PA's sister's alleged decision to not tell her brother about these threats "so as not to worry him"12 might be more believable if accompanied by supporting evidence that such information could have a serious detrimental effect on his mental or physical health, no such evidence has been provided. I note that the Appellant's sister has not explained in her letter why she decided to finally inform the PA about these events, notwithstanding her stated concerns for her brother's level of stress and anxiety. No apparent cultural explanation has been offered by the Appellants. Therefore, I find that the Appellants' explanation is outside the realm of what could reasonably be expected, and that it cannot be believed.

[17] For these reasons, I find that the Appellants have not credibly demonstrated that this evidence arose after the rejection of their claim or that the evidence was not reasonably available, or that they could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented at the time of the rejection.

[18] Furthermore, I find that this evidence is not sufficiently credible or trustworthy to be admissible. The jurisprudence supports that suspicious and fortuitous timing with respect to new evidence may, in limited circumstances, support a finding that it is not credible or trustworthy.13 I find that it is an extraordinary coincidence that the Appellants learned the identity of the APH and that the APH had suddenly escalated their apparent efforts to find them, just after their rejection by the RPD. This new evidence is extraordinarily fortuitous in that it directly responds to two of the main adverse findings by the RPD, that the Appellants did not know the identity of the criminal organization that targeted them, and that there was no evidence that the APH approached their family members to find them. If the new evidence is to be believed, the APH began persistently targeting the Appellants' family members more than a year after the Appellants' last interaction with them, and finally revealed themselves to be part of one of Mexico's most notorious cartels roughly two years after they began targeting the PA for extortion. Also, they located the PA's sister a few days after the RPD decision, even though she had moved and changed her number. These are sudden and unexplained developments that are so coincidental for the Appellants' claim that they must be treated with suspicion. This is in addition to the concerns I have identified above concerning the Appellants' explanation for not providing the evidence at the time of the RPD decision, which raise doubts about whether the events in question occurred. Overall, I find that the PA's letter is not sufficiently credible or trustworthy to be admitted.
[19] I accept that the letter is a sworn statement, however for the reasons provided herein, I find that there are good reasons to doubt the truthfulness of its contents.

[20] Therefore, I find that this evidence does not meet the requirements of s. 110(4) of the IRPA and I do not admit it.
ORAL HEARING

[21] The Appellants have requested an oral hearing. My jurisdiction to hold an oral hearing is limited to situations where admissible new evidence raises a serious issue of credibility; is central to the decision; and determinative of the claim.14
[22] There is no admissible new evidence in this claim. Therefore, I have no jurisdiction to hold a hearing.
ANALYSIS
[23] My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision after conducting an independent assessment.15

[24] The determinative issue in this claim is an IFA in Mérida, Yucatán.
There was no violation of procedural fairness or natural justice
[25] The Appellants argue that the RPD failed to provide the Appellant with notice that it was considering Mérida as a possible IFA, breaching their rights to procedural fairness and natural justice.

[26] They submit that as they were self-represented at the time, and the Immigration and Refugee Board should have provided a "screening form" to the Appellants before the RPD hearing which identified the relevant issues.

[27] The RPD identified an IFA in Mérida only at the outset of the hearing as one of the issues that it would be considering. The Appellants had little understanding of the issue, as corroborated by the fact that they later asked the RPD Member to explain why they were mentioning Mérida. The RPD Member did not address the Appellants' concerns during the hearing. The Appellants submit that they only obtained a solid understanding of IFA after they sought legal representation.
[28] The RPD Member did not ask the Appellants to make further submissions at the end of the hearing.
[29] I find that there is no merit to these arguments and that there was no violation of procedural fairness or natural justice.

[30] The jurisprudence establishes that notice of an IFA is sufficient when it is raised at the hearing and the claimant is afforded the opportunity to address the issue with evidence and argument.16 In this case, as the Appellants acknowledge, the RPD Member clearly raised the issue of an IFA in Mérida at the outset of the hearing. The Member also questioned both Appellants about the issue and gave them an opportunity to raise any additional questions or submissions.

[31] I disagree with the Appellants that the RPD ignored the PA's question during the RPD hearing about why the panel was mentioning Mérida. The record shows that when this was raised by the PA, the RPD used plain language to ask the PA why he could not live in Mérida, if he moved there to try to escape from the criminal group that he feared in his hometown.17 The RPD did not state the formal legal test for IFA laid out below, however it identified its concerns using simple language, and fully canvassed the issue during the hearing. I find no breach of procedural fairness or natural justice on the part of the RPD.

[32] The Appellants rely on Kamatasingh,18 noting that natural justice imposes an obligation on decision-makers to ensure the legal process is fair. I agree and affirm the principle in Kamatasingh that "[t]he paramount concern is ensuring a fair hearing where the unrepresented party will have the opportunity to fully present their case."19 However, the Appellants have not demonstrated that their hearing was unfair or that they did not have an opportunity to know the case to be met or to fully present their case. As already noted, the RPD Member clearly identified the issue of an IFA in Mérida at the commencement of the hearing and used plain language in expressing her concerns to the Appellants. I note that the Court also found in Kamatasingh that the RPD has no obligation to act as counsel for the Appellants, or to "teach" them the law.

[33] The Appellants also refer to Gomes20 and Kugapalan21 however I find that these cases do not square with the case before me and must be differentiated, since the tribunal did not give the applicants in those case any notice that it intended to consider the issue of IFA, either before or during the hearing. They also refer to Baker22 however they have not clearly explained how the RPD's decision goes against the principles established by that case. Fundamentally, the Appellants have not demonstrated that their procedural fairness rights were violated.

[34] Therefore, I find that there was no violation of procedural fairness or natural justice by the RPD.
The Appellants have a viable IFA in Mérida

[35] As per Rasaratnam,23 the two-pronged test for an IFA is as follows. The panel must be satisfied that:
(1) there is no serious possibility of the Appellant being persecuted or, on the balance of probabilities, in danger of torture or subjected to a risk to life or cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in the IFA,24 and
(2) that conditions in that part of the country are such that it would be reasonable, in all the circumstances, including those particular to the Appellant, for them to seek refuge there.25

[36] Once IFA is raised as an issue, the onus is on the Appellants to show that they do not have an IFA.26
The IFA meets the first prong of the test - the Appellants are not at risk in the IFA

[37] I have summarized the RPD's principal arguments as follows:
* The RPD accepted that the Appellants were victims of attempted extortion and were threatened and kidnapped by a local criminal gang or organization in XXXX and would be at risk if they returned there.
* However, the Appellants failed to establish that the APH have the motivation to pursue the Appellants to the IFA location.
* The Appellants testified that they do not know who threatened or kidnapped them, or the identity of the criminal gang that they fear.
* Even though the Appellants did not pay the ransom, and the APH threatened to kill them if they did not pay, they have not had any contact with the APH after they escaped.
* There is no evidence that the criminal gang contacted any of their family members in Mexico.
* The APH's interest in the Appellants was local, financial, and did not persist after the PA ceased the operation of his business.
* The Appellants' belief that the threats would continue in the IFA is based on speculation.
* The objective documentary evidence does not establish or support that they would be target of a nationwide search by the APH, given their profile.

[38] I have summarized the Appellant's arguments as follows:
* The identity and motivation of the APH is established by the new evidence from the PA's sister.
* The objective documentary evidence indicates that organized crime groups may be motivated to track and retaliate against a person outside their operating area for refusing to make payments.27
* The RPD neglected to consider the Appellants' overall circumstances and the interest of the APH in finding the Appellants because they escaped without paying the ransom.
* Nowhere in the PA's BOC does it state that the motivations of the APH are confined to his operation of his XXXX XXXX business. They note that the PA worked as an XXXX XXXX for the XXXX XXXX, which allowed him to travel and have good standard of living.
* The Appellant provides objective documentary evidence about the national power and reach of the CJNG, which extends to Yucatán. He submits that it would be unreasonable to relocate to a territory where the APH are among the dominant criminal actors.
* The Appellants would have to provide their voting card/CURP documents in the IFA location, which would give the CJNG a direct link to their whereabouts, given the objective documentary evidence about data security or lack thereof and high levels of official corruption in Mexico. Their life would be tantamount to living in hiding.
* It is an error for the RPD to draw a negative credibility inference on the basis of absence of corroborating evidence.
* The Appellants do not have access to adequate state protection in Mexico.

[39] I agree with the RPD for the same reasons it had provided and am not persuaded by the Appellants' arguments. I find that the Appellants failed to establish that the APH possess sufficient motivation to pursue them to Mérida.

[40] The RPD correctly determined that the Appellants were unable to identify the criminal organization that targeted them and did not adduce sufficient credible evidence that the APH are something other than a local criminal gang in Morelos. The Appellants do not challenge this, their argument is that they only learned that the APH are the CJNG after their refusal by the RPD. My reasons for rejecting this new evidence have already been explained above.

[41] The jurisprudence establishes that the burden is on the Appellants to establish the identity of the APH.28 Failure to do so undermines their argument that the APH have the means and the motivation to find and harm them anywhere in the country. As the Court noted in Morales Esquivel, "...if the applicants did not know the identity of their aggressors' gang, how could they claim that an unknown gang would target them throughout the whole country?"29

[42] The RPD correctly found that the fact that the APH made no apparent efforts to contact them or their family members after they escaped from the gang without paying the ransom indicates a lack of motivation on the part of the APH to pursue the Appellants to the IFA location. The Appellants escaped their kidnappers in XXXX 2021 and left Mexico about a month later. Their claims were heard by the RPD nearly two years later in February 2023. During the intervening period, there is no admissible or credible evidence that the APH contacted the Appellants or their family members, even though the PA's sister was originally approached by the APH for the ransom payment. The Court has found that in assessing motivation, the Board may take into consideration the fact that the agents of harm did not bother the Appellants in the months before her departure to Canada even though they were not in hiding or contact her family members.30

[43] I agree with the Appellants that the objective documentary evidence establishes that "[i]f a criminal group has "very strong motivation to find and retaliate against a certain person" then, depending on the circumstances, "[the ability to track or retaliate against a certain person] would be a reasonable concern to have."31 However, this must be put into context. The same objective documentary evidence indicates that the risk of being tracked by a criminal group depends on whether the criminal group is one of the more powerful groups in Mexico, or if there are indications of having cooperation with the authorities. Additionally, "...it is an oversimplification to say that a group will track just anyone. It really depends on who you are and what you did... Similarly [according to another source] the safety of an individual who relocates to flee from one of these organizations' threats depend on the interests a group may have to punish or retaliate against them..."32

[44] In this case, the Appellants have not demonstrated that the APH are a powerful crime group in Mexico or have influence over the authorities. As they do not know the identity of the APH, they have also not established that they have an interest in finding and retaliating against the Appellants in another part of Mexico. As already noted, there is no evidence that the APH attempted to contact them or their family members after they escaped from them without paying their ransom. Overall, I find that the Appellants have not established that the APH have sufficient motivation to pursue them to the IFA location, merely for refusing their demand to pay a ransom.

[45] I agree with the Appellants that the RPD was speculating that the APH were only interested in the Appellants' family XXXX XXXX business. By the same token, I find that the Appellants are merely speculating that the APH were motivated to kidnap the PA because of his well-paid occupation as an XXXX, or that their failure to pay the ransom for their abduction in XXXX 2021 would be sufficient to motivate them to embark on a nationwide search for the Appellants.

[46] It is unclear what the Appellants mean when they argue that the RPD failed to consider their overall circumstances in assessing the motivation of the APH. It is the Appellant who bears the burden of establishing that the APH possess the motivation to pursue them to the IFA, and I find no error on the part of the RPD here. I find that the RPD considered all the relevant circumstances before it.

[47] I find that the Appellants are speculating that the APH would gain "a direct link to their whereabouts"33 when they provide their personal identity documents to work, vote, etc. in the IFA location. Fundamentally, the Appellants have not established that the APH would be motivated to attempt to obtain such information on the black market in Mexico for personal data or exploit the high levels of official corruption in Mexico for this purpose.

[48] The Appellants refer to case law indicating that it is an error for the RPD to draw a negative credibility inference on the basis of absence of corroborating evidence. I do not dispute this case law however the Appellants have not explained how this is relevant to their case. The Appellants have not identified any specific errors on the part of the RPD, and none emerge perceptibly from the record. In fact, the RPD affirmed the credibility of their core allegations, and did not draw any negative inferences from the absence of corroborative evidence.
[49] Similarly, I find that the Appellants' arguments relating to state protection in Mexico are not relevant. The determinative issue in this case is IFA, not state protection.
[50] The Appellants have also raised concerns related to gender-based violence against the Associate Appellant (AA) in the IFA location. I have addressed these in the section that follows.

[51] Therefore, I find that the Appellants have failed to establish that the agents of persecution or harm have both the means and the motivation to pursue them to Mérida. The Appellants have not demonstrated that they face a serious possibility of persecution, or that, on a balance of probabilities, they would be subject personally to a danger of torture, or to a risk to their life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in Mérida.
The IFA meets the second prong of the test - the IFA is not unreasonable

[52] The RPD correctly determined that the Appellants did not meet their burden of establishing that it would be unreasonable, in all the circumstances, including those particular to the Appellants, to relocate to Mérida.

[53] The RPD considered the Appellants' language ability (Spanish), education (bachelor's degree in XXXX for PA; college degree for AA), employment experience in Mexico (PA worked for a company as an XXXX and had his own business as a XXXX; AA worked for the XXXX XXXX). The RPD found that the Appellants had transferable education and employment skills developed in Mexico that would assist them in their relocation to Mérida.

[54] The RPD found that the Appellants would not face serious barriers with respect to language, employment, housing, religion, or culture in the IFA location. The RPD noted that when questioned, the Appellants did not identify any obstacles to securing accommodation or social services.

[55] The RPD acknowledged that relocation naturally involves difficulties, however under the circumstances, it found that this would not constitute undue hardship that would render the IFA unreasonable.

[56] The Appellants argue that the RPD committed two errors in its assessment of the second prong of the IFA. Firstly, it failed to apply the Chairperson's Guideline on Gender Considerations in Proceedings Before the Board (Gender Guidelines)34 while weighing the evidence and country conditions with regard to the prevalence of feminicide in Mexico and the IFA location. Secondly, it did not conduct a proper analysis of the Appellants' situation based on the cost of living, employment prospects, housing, access to social services, and education.

[57] Respectfully, I find no error on the part of the RPD with respect to the application of the Gender Guidelines. The AA is female however no gender considerations were raised by the Appellants, and none emerge perceptibly from the record. The Appellants did not express any fears relating to gender-based violence or the prevalence of feminicide in Mexico.

[58] Notwithstanding this, I have considered and applied the Gender Guidelines in respect of the AA's particular circumstances and the objective documentary evidence concerning feminicide in Mexico. As the Appellants point out, feminicide, and violence against women, in general, is a form of gender-based persecution. Evidence in the National Document Package corroborates that feminicide, the intentional killing of women because they are women, is a serious and persistent human rights problem affecting every state in Mexico,35 and that there is frequently impunity for perpetrators.36

[59] The Appellants submit that the AA would be at risk of gender-based violence in Mérida, further noting that the Appellants were already victims of kidnapping, and that Mérida is the city in Yucatán with the highest percentage of homicides. 31 of the state's 45 registered murders occurred there.

[60] While I find that the risk to the AA of gender-based violence in the IFA location cannot be positively ruled out, the Appellants have not demonstrated that this risk rises to more than a mere possibility of persecution on a Convention ground, given the objective documentary evidence about the recorded numbers of feminicides in the country,37 and the general homicide rate in Mérida noted by the Appellant. I accept that the AA, like the PA, was a victim of kidnapping, however there is no evidence before me that this was motivated by gender or involved gender-based violence. There is no evidence before me that the AA fears domestic violence or has been a victim of gender-based violence.

[61] Nor do I agree with the Appellants that the RPD failed to conduct a proper analysis of their situation. It is true, as the Appellants point out, that the RPD "cannot base a finding that there is an IFA without sufficient evidence, solely on the basis that the claimant has not fulfilled the onus of proof."38 As already noted, the RPD considered the Appellants' evidence about their personal circumstances, and their testimony about why they believed that they could not relocate to Mérida, before determining that the IFA was not unreasonable. The Appellants did not provide any evidence to support their submissions on appeal that the IFA would be unaffordable, or that they would be unable to secure employment or housing, or access education or social services.

[62] The Gender Guidelines outlines various gender considerations that decision-makers should consider in assessing the reasonableness of an IFA. For example, single women with or without children, may face various and compounded obstacles rendering an IFA unreasonable. In this case, no such concerns have been identified by the Appellants, and I note that the Appellants are a male-female couple without children.

[63] The Appellants face a high burden to show that the IFA is unreasonable. They have not met this burden by providing actual and concrete evidence of adverse conditions that would jeopardize their life and safety in relocating to the IFA.
[64] I agree with the RPD's findings for the same reasons it provides.
[65] I find that the Appellants have not demonstrated that it would be objectively unreasonable or unduly harsh for them to relocate to Mérida.
CONCLUSION
[66] Therefore, I find that the Appellants have a viable IFA in Mérida, Yucatán.

[67] I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.
